summary:
La Araucanía is a region of Chile, and a trans visitor there stands under Chile's national statutory framework rather than any regional variant. Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019: adults may change registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, applicants aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and those under 14 fall outside the statute although it recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in the case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

Anti-discrimination and hate-crime rules are national. The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Detention conditions follow a protocol signed by the national director of Gendarmería de Chile, guaranteeing recognition of a trans detainee's gender identity, placement by assumed gender, segmented housing, rules for entry examinations and for trans visitors, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation.

Healthcare access is governed nationally. The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, while the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law; the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres, and the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. Chile's Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, recommending elimination of the Gender Identity Support Program, restriction of minors' progressive autonomy, a ban on hormonal treatment for minors and repeal of the circular protecting gender identity in schools. The report does not change the law.

Transphobic violence is documented in Chile. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime, with the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessing. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Within that national picture, La Araucanía is the region where recorded homo- and transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025. Movilh's XXIV annual human-rights report, published on 24 March 2026 with 2025 data, recorded a 150% year-on-year increase in the region and ranked it first in growth nationally, with the region accounting for 1.96% of the national case total. The same report put the national total at a record 3,620 documented cases, 27.1% above the 2024 figure, with 2025 alone representing 23% of all cases recorded across the 24-year series. A visitor to La Araucanía therefore faces a national legal environment that recognises gender identity and a regional trend line in reported homo- and transphobic incidents moving faster than anywhere else in Chile.
tangentialFactors:
The regional spike reported by Movilh sits on a small base: La Araucanía represented 1.96% of the national case total in 2025, so a 150% year-on-year increase describes rapid growth in a comparatively small share of documented incidents rather than the largest absolute volume in the country.

Chile's national totals are themselves at a record. Movilh documented 3,620 cases in 2025, 27.1% above 2024, and that single year accounts for 23% of everything recorded in the organisation's 24-year series, a pattern consistent with rising willingness to report as much as with rising incidence.

Two branches of Chilean state practice have recently diverged on trans minors. The Constitutional Court struck down a budget provision barring the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents on 9 January 2025 by seven votes to three, while Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program in November 2025 and the Chamber of Deputies endorsed a non-binding report favouring bans on hormonal treatment for minors on 15 May 2025. Court rulings and statutes bind; commission reports and budget lines do not operate as prohibitions on private medical care.

Regional comparison is thin. The inventory supplies La Araucanía's growth ranking and share of the national total but does not set out figures for other regions, so the region's standing relative to Santiago or other high-incident areas is not sourced.
localsOnly:
Residents of La Araucanía use the same national machinery as everyone else in Chile. Adults change name and sex directly at the Civil Registry; 14 to 18-year-olds must go through family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and those under 14 cannot use the statute, though the 9 April 2025 Constitutional Court decision declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable in the specific case before it and does not generally open the law to younger children.

Registered trans residents are protected at work and in services by the Zamudio Law as extended to gender expression in 2018, and bias motivation aggravates criminal sentencing. Hate-motivated violence can therefore be charged and sentenced as an aggravated offence rather than as a bare assault.

People held in the region's detention facilities are covered by the Gendarmería de Chile protocol on gender identity, which provides placement by assumed gender, segmented housing, regulated entry examinations and access rules for trans visitors, with a standing committee monitoring implementation.

Medical care for trans residents is provided through the public system, which has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and facilities must record patients under their social name under the 2011 Ministry of Health circular. The Ministry of Health-run support programme continues after Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program in November 2025, and Crece con Orgullo has served children and adolescents aged 3 to 17 since 2023. The June 2024 circular's suggestion to defer new hormone blockers or cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are issued is a recommendation, and the Medical College has stated that physicians may still prescribe.

Same-sex couples may marry and adopt jointly, and civil unions have been available since 2015.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Movilh figures are documented cases and complaints compiled by an LGBT rights organisation, not police arrest, charge or conviction statistics. Whether reported incidents in La Araucanía resulted in prosecutions, or whether regional police use the hate-crime aggravation in practice, is not sourced in the inventory.

No figures are available for other Chilean regions, so La Araucanía's 150% growth cannot be positioned against absolute case volumes elsewhere.

The inventory does not state whether the Gendarmería protocol has been implemented at specific facilities in La Araucanía, nor whether surgical or endocrine services for trans patients are available within the region or require travel to Santiago.

Regional-level reporting on the two documented national acts of transphobic violence places them outside La Araucanía; no trans-specific homicide or assault in the region is sourced for the period covered.

Whether the restrictive measures endorsed by the Chamber of Deputies on 15 May 2025 will be taken up as legislation is unresolved on this inventory; as of the sources cited they remain recommendations without legal effect.
